config.title: useReducer vs useState

intro.title: useReducer vs useState
intro.body: In this lesson, you will build a simple counter application to compare two React hooks: useState and useReducer. You will learn the core concept of state management by implementing the same counter functionality with both hooks side by side. The main technologies involved are React functional components, the useState hook for simple state, and the useReducer hook for more complex state logic. This will help you understand when to choose each hook based on your application's needs, using TypeScript for type safety in an Angular-track context that emphasizes structured state handling.
intro.usecase: In Angular applications, managing complex component state is crucial for features like multi-step forms, shopping carts, or dashboard controls. For instance, a flight booking form with passenger details, seat selection, and payment steps benefits from useReducer to handle interdependent state transitions cleanly. Similarly, an e-commerce product filter panel with multiple toggles, price ranges, and category selections becomes more maintainable with reducer patterns. Developers choose useReducer over simple useState when state logic involves multiple sub-values or complex transitions, making real-world UI components more predictable and easier to debug.

objectives: Implement a useState hook to manage simple component state in Angular
Construct a useReducer hook to handle complex state logic with multiple actions
Configure state updates using both useState's setter function and useReducer's dispatch method
Bind component UI elements to state values managed by both hooks
Control component behavior by dispatching specific action types with useReducer
Initialize state with different data structures appropriate for each hook
Render dynamic content based on state changes from both useState and useReducer

steps.title: Import Component, CommonModule, FormsModule, and NgIf
steps.instruction: Import Component from '@angular/core', CommonModule and FormsModule from '@angular/forms', and NgIf from '@angular/common'.
steps.hint: Use the import keyword followed by the symbol name and the module path. Separate multiple imports with commas.
steps.seedCode: // Import Component from '@angular/core', CommonModule and FormsModule from '@angular/forms', and NgIf from '@angular/common'
steps.expectedOutcome: The necessary Angular modules and directives are imported for building the component.
successCriteria: Component is imported from '@angular/core', CommonModule and FormsModule are imported from '@angular/forms', and NgIf is imported from '@angular/common'.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You imported some of the required modules. Make sure to import Component, CommonModule, FormsModule, and NgIf.
steps.feedbackWrong: The imports are missing or incorrect. Check the module paths and symbol names.

steps.title: Create the main component class
steps.instruction: Create a class named CounterComponent and decorate it with @Component, setting selector to 'app-counter' and template to an empty string.
steps.hint: Use the @Component decorator from '@angular/core' and define the class with the specified selector and template.
steps.expectedOutcome: The CounterComponent class is defined with the @Component decorator, ready for state and UI implementation.
successCriteria: CounterComponent class exists with @Component decorator, selector 'app-counter', and template ''.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've started the component, but ensure the @Component decorator has selector 'app-counter' and template ''.
steps.feedbackWrong: Check that you created a class named CounterComponent with the @Component decorator and the specified selector and template.

steps.title: Add imports array to component decorator
steps.instruction: In the @Component decorator, add an imports array containing CommonModule and FormsModule.
steps.hint: The imports array should be placed inside the @Component decorator object, after the selector property.
steps.expectedOutcome: The component decorator will have an imports array with CommonModule and FormsModule registered.
successCriteria: The @Component decorator contains an imports array with CommonModule and FormsModule.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure you've added an imports array with both CommonModule and FormsModule inside the @Component decorator.
steps.feedbackWrong: The imports array is missing or incomplete. Check that you've added both CommonModule and FormsModule to the imports array in the @Component decorator.

steps.title: Initialize useState counter
steps.instruction: In the CounterComponent class, declare a property called useCounter and initialize it to 0.
steps.hint: Add a property directly in the class body, like: useCounter = 0;
steps.expectedOutcome: The CounterComponent class now has a useCounter property with initial value 0.
successCriteria: The useCounter property is declared in the CounterComponent class and initialized to 0.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you've declared the useCounter property and initialized it to exactly 0 in the CounterComponent class.
steps.feedbackWrong: The useCounter property isn't properly declared or initialized. In Angular components, you declare properties directly in the class body and initialize them with values.

steps.title: Define useState increment handler
steps.instruction: Inside the CounterComponent class, create a method called incrementUseState that adds 1 to the useCounter property.
steps.hint: Define a method with no parameters that increments the useCounter property by 1.
steps.expectedOutcome: The CounterComponent class will have an incrementUseState method that increments the useCounter property.
successCriteria: The incrementUseState method is defined in the CounterComponent class and increments useCounter by 1.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure your method is named incrementUseState and it adds 1 to the useCounter property.
steps.feedbackWrong: The incrementUseState method is not correctly defined. Check that it's inside the CounterComponent class and properly increments useCounter.

steps.title: Define useState decrement handler
steps.instruction: Inside the CounterComponent class, define a method called decrementUseState that subtracts 1 from the useCounter property.
steps.hint: Create a method that updates the useCounter property by decreasing its value by 1.
steps.expectedOutcome: The component will have a decrementUseState method that decreases the useCounter value by 1 when called.
successCriteria: A method named decrementUseState is defined in CounterComponent and it subtracts 1 from useCounter.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've created a method, but make sure it's named decrementUseState and it subtracts 1 from useCounter.
steps.feedbackWrong: The decrementUseState method is not correctly defined. Check that it's inside CounterComponent and properly updates useCounter.

steps.title: Initialize useReducer state
steps.instruction: Inside the CounterComponent class, declare a property called reducerState with the initial value {count: 0}.
steps.hint: Add a property declaration in the class body, similar to how you declared useCounter earlier. Use the appropriate type annotation.
steps.expectedOutcome: The reducerState property is initialized with {count: 0} in the CounterComponent class.
successCriteria: The reducerState property is declared with the initial value {count: 0}.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure you've declared a property called reducerState with the exact initial value {count: 0}.
steps.feedbackWrong: The reducerState property isn't properly initialized. Check that you've declared it with {count: 0} as the initial value.

steps.title: Define useReducer reducer function
steps.instruction: In the CounterComponent class, define a method called counterReducer that takes a CounterState object and a CounterAction object as parameters, and returns a new CounterState based on the action type.
steps.hint: The reducer should handle both 'increment' and 'decrement' action types. Use a switch statement or if/else to check action.type and return the appropriate new state.
steps.expectedOutcome: The component will have a reducer function that can process state updates based on action types.
successCriteria: A method named counterReducer is defined with proper TypeScript parameter types (CounterState, CounterAction) and returns CounterState, handling both action types.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure your counterReducer method has the correct parameter types and handles both action types properly.
steps.feedbackWrong: The reducer function isn't defined correctly. Check that you've created a method called counterReducer with the right parameters and return type.

steps.title: Define useReducer dispatch handlers
steps.instruction: In the CounterComponent class, define two methods: incrementReducer() and decrementReducer(). Each method should call counterReducer with the appropriate action object.
steps.hint: Create methods that dispatch actions to your reducer. For increment, pass { type: 'INCREMENT' }. For decrement, pass { type: 'DECREMENT' }.
steps.expectedOutcome: Two methods are added to the CounterComponent class that dispatch actions to the reducer function.
successCriteria: The CounterComponent class contains incrementReducer() and decrementReducer() methods that call counterReducer with appropriate action objects.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've created at least one dispatch method, but both incrementReducer and decrementReducer are needed.
steps.feedbackWrong: The dispatch methods are not properly defined. Make sure you create both incrementReducer() and decrementReducer() methods that call counterReducer with action objects.

steps.title: Create template with both counters and buttons
steps.instruction: Add the template to your component to display both counters and their respective increment/decrement buttons.
steps.hint: Use Angular's template syntax with interpolation {{ }} to display the counter values and (click) event bindings for the buttons.
steps.analogousExample:
// Example: Template with two sections

useState Counter

Count: {{ useStateCounter }}

useReducer Counter

Count: {{ reducerState.count }}
steps.expectedOutcome: The component will have a complete template showing both counters with their current values and functional buttons to increment/decrement each counter.
successCriteria: Template contains two sections (useState and useReducer), displays both counter values using interpolation, and has buttons with (click) event bindings to the appropriate handler methods.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but check that you have both counter sections, proper interpolation for values, and correct (click) event bindings for all buttons.
steps.feedbackWrong: The template is missing required elements. Make sure to include both counter sections with values displayed and buttons with event handlers.
